tweets.text:
We invited Claude users to share how they use AI, what they dream it could make possible, and what they fear it might do.

Nearly 81,000 people responded in one week—the largest qualitative study of its kind.

Read more: https://t.co/tmp2RnZxRm

New on the Engineering Blog: How we designed Claude Code auto mode.

Many Claude Code users let Claude work without permission prompts. Auto mode is a safer middle ground: we built and tested classifiers that make approval decisions instead.

Read more: https://t.co/dpcMcWMf5k

We find that since November 2025, consumer use has become less concentrated: the top 10 tasks now make up 19% of conversations, down from 24%. We also see a rise in personal queries, and continued convergence in adoption rates in the US.

Read more: https://t.co/9UUq3UsnLi

New from the Anthropic Economic Index: how people’s use of Claude changes with experience.

Longer-term users are more likely to iterate carefully with Claude, and less likely to hand it full autonomy. They attempt higher-value tasks, and receive more successful responses. https://t.co/yCsrA0bLt9

New on the Anthropic Engineering Blog: 

How we use a multi-agent harness to push Claude further in frontend design and long-running autonomous software engineering.

Read more: https://t.co/HWvmXk1ykn

Models keep improving on long-horizon tasks, but splitting work across many agents doesn’t suit every problem. 

We walk through the setup for a single agent working sequentially on a task where mistakes compound: modeling the early universe. 

Read more:
https://t.co/7rrQY2vp9H

We’re launching with two new posts.

Can AI do theoretical physics? 

Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz led Claude Opus 4.5 through a graduate-level calculation. AI can’t yet do original work autonomously, but it can vastly accelerate it. 

Read more: https://t.co/UUfFuLqhb7

Introducing the Anthropic Science Blog.

Increasing the pace of scientific progress is a core part of Anthropic’s mission. The Science Blog will feature new research and stories of how scientists are using AI to accelerate their work.

Read the intro: https://t.co/1P9BDyX3xG

Thank you to the 80,508 people who took the time to speak with us. It has been striking, and humbling, to see how AI figures in so many people’s hopes, fears, and dreams.

Read the full post here: https://t.co/tmp2RnZxRm

These interviews capture texture that surveys can’t. They render in detail how people worldwide are already experiencing AI's opportunities and risks.

We plan to use Anthropic Interviewer regularly, on different topics, to help inform how AI can be built to benefit everyone.
Globally, 67% of people view AI positively, but optimism runs higher in South America, Africa, and Asia than in Europe or the United States. https://t.co/3QkawqnJY0

What people wanted and feared from AI appeared tightly bound. Those who benefited the most from AI in a given area were also the most likely to fear what it could cost them.

But while mentions of benefits tend to be grounded in experience, fears were more often anticipatory. https://t.co/EZIA1Q9kMN

Hopes clustered around a few basic desires, but concerns about AI were more varied. Most common were AI unreliability, jobs and the economy, and maintaining human autonomy and agency. 

Notably, economic concern was the strongest predictor of overall AI sentiment. https://t.co/UGmP67a5j6
When Claude asked whether AI had taken a step towards fulfilling the vision they described, 81% of people said yes. https://t.co/nBicy2wBPc

What do people most want from AI?

Roughly one third want AI to improve their quality of life—to find more time, achieve financial security, or carve out mental bandwidth. Another quarter want AI to help them do better and more fulfilling work. https://t.co/UgMD53igv7

To do research at this scale, we used Anthropic Interviewer—a version of Claude prompted to conduct a conversational interview. We heard from people across 159 countries in 70 different languages. 

Browse some of their quotes here: https://t.co/JAavqGYxME https://t.co/auyrssDFat

The open source ecosystem underpins nearly every software system in the world. As AI grows more capable, open source security becomes increasingly important.

We're donating to the Linux Foundation to continue to help secure the foundations AI runs on.

https://t.co/xoyjNFcSlY

The Institute will be led by @jackclarkSF, in a new role as Anthropic’s Head of Public Benefit. It'll bring together an interdisciplinary staff of machine learning engineers, economists, and social scientists, making full use of the inside information of a frontier AI lab.

We believe being forewarned is being forearmed. The Anthropic Institute will tell the world what we are seeing and expecting from the technology we build.

@shailenewoodley The National Geographic 33—inspired by our 33 founders—is an initiative honoring changemakers who are rising to meet the most critical challenges of our time, making meaningful progress and incredible breakthroughs.

National Geographic 33 changemaker @shailenewoodley has been a fierce advocate for a global agreement that will establish legal frameworks to protect international marine areas. Learn more about her efforts to protect our oceans: https://t.co/tReer7eHxD #NatGeo33 https://t.co/SNAJMhczOm

The National Geographic 33—inspired by our 33 founders—is an initiative honoring changemakers who are rising to meet the most critical challenges of our time, making meaningful progress and incredible breakthroughs.
Now his work is taking shape outside of Africa as he designs major projects in Las Vegas, Rio de Janeiro, and beyond, building in ways that complement nature rather than fight against it.

The first African laureate of the prestigious Pritzker Prize, architect and National Geographic 33 changemaker Francis Kéré has long been praised for his approach to energy efficiency in his projects. Learn more about Kéré's work: https://t.co/3ON2TMoTF8 #NatGeo33 https://t.co/hLpNgCUxOg

@borgeousland The National Geographic 33—inspired by our 33 founders—is an initiative honoring changemakers who are rising to meet the most critical challenges of our time, making meaningful progress and incredible breakthroughs.

@borgeousland These National Geographic 33 changemakers are on a quest to ski across the world’s 20 largest ice fields and collect ice samples to aid glaciologists’ understanding of how climate change affects places rarely visited by humans.

When National Geographic Explorer @borgeousland pulled his adventuring partner Vincent Colliard out of a crevasse on Ellesmere Island, it nearly ruined the longest expedition of their Ice Legacy Project. Read more about their work: https://t.co/DfeuICigCB #NatGeo33 https://t.co/RM2x0CHWsR

National Geographic Explorer Biruté Galdikas has passed away at the age of 79. One of the so-called Trimates, alongside Dian Fossey and Jane Goodall, she conducted the first long-term study of orangutans. Read her iconic 1975 National Geographic cover story: https://t.co/Q1BlsxwjsA

@paulakahumbu @wildlifedirect The National Geographic 33—inspired by our 33 founders—is an initiative honoring changemakers who are rising to meet the most critical challenges of our time, making meaningful progress and incredible breakthroughs.

@paulakahumbu She pushed the Kenyan legal system to aggressively prosecute ivory poachers and hosted Africa’s first nature-documentary TV series made by Africans. Her organization, @WildlifeDirect, created a suite of short films to promote a new platform for reporting environmental crimes.

National Geographic 33 changemaker and National Geographic Explorer @paulakahumbu is a trailblazer for conservation efforts in Africa. Learn more about Kahumbu’s campaigns on behalf of wildlife: https://t.co/BQg2AyH24M #NatGeo33 https://t.co/iR9LcPPw8Y

The National Geographic 33—inspired by our 33 founders—is an initiative honoring changemakers who are rising to meet the most critical challenges of our time, making meaningful progress and incredible breakthroughs.
Some overlooked wild plants, she says, may be “not only a way to diversify our diet but to make our agriculture more resilient.”

Botanist, National Geographic 33 changemaker, and National Geographic Explorer Benedetta Gori says modern agriculture grows too few crops, leaving it vulnerable to climate change and disease. Read more about her work: https://t.co/urZTzhjUSU #NatGeo33 https://t.co/MRFCrfVKok

@starwars The National Geographic 33—inspired by our 33 founders—is an initiative honoring changemakers who are rising to meet the most critical challenges of our time, making meaningful progress and incredible breakthroughs.
@starwars The duo’s authentic approach to travel content is the ultimate antidote to today’s overly polished vacation posts on social media.
In Long Way Home, the new installment of his Long Way television series, the @starwars actor set out on a 7,000-mile transcontinental motorcycle trip with fellow actor Charley Boorman.
